title: The Cloud as a Type of Baptism
english: …coming with the clouds (Daniel 7:13), and he set down what follows. Ezekiel likewise says that he saw a firmament with the seraphim beneath it, and on the throne he saw a man, or rather the likeness of a man, whose upper parts, he says, resembled amber, while from the loins to the feet he was like the appearance of fire (Ezekiel 1:22–27).

In each of these visions he subtly hints to us at an image of the glory that befits God and of the mystery of Christ. Nothing, then, prevents us from understanding that here too the Lord was seen on a light cloud for a most useful and necessary purpose. For the cloud fills out for us a type of spiritual rain and dew, and of saving baptism itself.

Indeed, the blessed Paul says that those of Israel's blood were baptized in the cloud and in the sea (1 Corinthians 10:2). As they crossed that deep desert, the cloud hung over them by day, and by night a pillar of fire went before them (Exodus 13:21). Through both of these Christ was being portrayed, that is, the mystery concerning him: justification and sanctification in faith and holy baptism.

So the Lord, coming to cleanse and transform the Egyptians, in a manner fitting God and spiritually, of course, had to be seen on a light cloud. For there was no other way to scrub from the soul of those in error the stain ingrained in it except through holy baptism; and we hold that the cloud is a type of that baptism.

And the cloud is very fittingly called light. For we are baptized for the putting away of sin; and as we turn away from ungodliness as from a burden truly hard to carry, we become, in a way, winged by this, and learn to set our minds on things above (Colossians 3:2) and to keep our hearts on high.

As for the Lord's sitting upon the cloud, I think it shows this: sitting hints to us at either rest or authority. So Christ rests, not in any way in worship according to the law, but rather in the perfection that comes through holy baptism; and in this way he has come to reign over those on earth.

He says that the handmade things of Egypt will be shaken before his face (Isaiah 19:1). For once holy baptism had been revealed and Christ had shone forth, it was wholly necessary that the playthings of the ancient deceit should vanish and the snares of the devil be seen broken to pieces.

For the devil had caught in his net, for ruin and destruction, practically every nation and race, but the Egyptians more than the rest. They were the most superstitious of all, perhaps outdoing even the Persians and Assyrians in error, although the God-inspired Scripture says of those peoples' land that it is a land of carved images (Jeremiah 50:38).
He says that the heart of the Egyptians will be overcome, yielding, as I think…
translator_notes: Copy-text: PG 70, Commentary on Isaiah (CPG 5203). The section begins mid-word ('…of Man coming with the clouds') and ends mid-sentence.
Cyril names the seraphim beneath Ezekiel's firmament; Ezekiel 1 speaks of living creatures. The English follows Cyril.
Jeremiah 50:38 is Jeremiah 27:38 in the Septuagint.

title: Five Cities That Swear by the Lord
english: …we say that the first is what is now the city of the Rhinocorurans. They do indeed speak the Canaanite tongue (Isaiah 19:18), for the people in these cities have taken pains to adopt not so much the speech of the Egyptians as that of the Syrians.

Some say that Josephus clearly records in his own writings that a certain Ionias, who was of the blood of Levi and honoured with the priesthood under the law, left the land of the Jews, either after quarrelling with some of his own people or perhaps after suffering persecution, and occupied these five cities, since they bordered on the Canaanites. This man, he says, gathered a multitude of Jews past easy counting and settled in one of these five cities, which was also named the city of Asedek, that is, of righteousness (Isaiah 19:18). From that time, they say, those living at the borders of Egypt grew accustomed to speaking the language of the Canaanites and came to love it.

And they will learn, he says, to swear by the name of the Lord (Isaiah 19:18). This too is remarkable. For worshippers of vain things are accustomed to swear by whichever element of the world each of them fancies. Some name heaven, others the sun, others even the handmade things in their shrines; but they make no mention at all of the true God, for they have not known him. But to swear by his name belongs to those who have already come to know him and believe.

So too the all-wise Moses, when Israel had come away from the worship of Egypt, led them to the knowledge of the true God, saying: “You shall worship the Lord your God, and him only shall you serve”; and he added to this: “And by his name you shall swear” (Deuteronomy 6:13). That these five cities swear by no vain thing, but rather take up the name of the Lord for their oaths, is therefore clear proof that they received the faith.
“On that day there will be an altar to the Lord in the land of Egypt, and a pillar to the Lord at its border; and it will be a sign to the Lord for ever in the land of Egypt” (Isaiah 19:19–20).

For the whole land of the Egyptians was crowded with temples and full of altars, and there were libations and sacrifices everywhere, offered by them partly to the elements of the world and partly, as I said, to the statues set up in shrines, and indeed to the pillars of demons. And why do I say this, when they even set up the shapes of irrational animals and bestowed on them the glory that befits God?

See, then, from what to what the state of the Egyptians has changed. For those who were once more superstitious than all others, and had plunged without bridle into lawless excess, will on that day, he says, that is, at that time when the saving preaching shines among them, accept the worship of him who by nature…
translator_notes: Copy-text: PG 70, Commentary on Isaiah (CPG 5203). The section begins and ends mid-sentence.
Ionias is the form in the Greek here; the priest meant is evidently Onias, who according to Josephus founded a temple in Egypt. 'Of the blood of Levi' reads the printed 'ἐξαίμασι' as 'ἐξ αἵματος'.
Cyril's form of Deuteronomy 6:13 ('worship… him only') agrees with the wording quoted in Matthew 4:10.

title: The Assyrian Laments Before the Battle
english: …and they will march on and pass through the desert. “As if a storm of winds should pass through the desert” (Isaiah 21:1), raising the dust and all but throwing everything into confusion.

He adds: “For the vision is fearful, and a harsh one was announced to me” (Isaiah 21:1–2). For the mere sight of the enemy alone, and a most valiant host of fighting men equipped for war, is quite enough to strike harsh fear into those who see it. Yet he does not say only that he saw it, but also, “It was announced to me”; for together with the sight he was taught the outcome of events, plainly by God.

“The one who deals faithlessly deals faithlessly, and the lawless one acts lawlessly” (Isaiah 21:2). The boldness of the attackers, he says, cannot be checked. For no human reasoning kindles them to gentleness; no one among them gives thought to what is right, but each acts lawlessly without restraint and deals faithlessly as he pleases, with no mercy in him. For they do not look to mercy; rather, he says, their whole eager work will be to act lawlessly and faithlessly.

He said something similar through the voice of the same prophet to the inhabitants of the Assyrians' land: “Behold, I am bringing the Medes against you, who do not value silver and have no need of gold. They will shatter the arrows of young men” (Isaiah 13:17–18). For when God brings wrath on those who sin, nothing will be able to help. Rather, a mind like a wild beast's takes up its dwelling in those who are bent on ravaging whomever they rush against.

“The Elamites are upon me, and the envoys of the Persians are coming against me. Now I will groan and comfort myself. Therefore my loins are filled with faintness, and pangs have seized me like a woman in labour. I did wrong so as not to hear; I hastened so as not to see. My heart wanders, and lawlessness plunges me under; my soul is set in fear” (Isaiah 21:2–4).

The words here have the force of a speech put in a character's mouth. For the Assyrian is brought on stage, fearing the assault, well aware of the enemy's ranks and of whom their war is aimed at. “Not against any others,” he says, “but against me the Elamites and the very best of the Persians have set out. So I will groan and comfort myself.”

For those who have fallen into the worst misfortune seem to find some kind of comfort in lamenting and wailing, since pain squeezes out tears. Yet it is a strange thing if the Assyrians lament, since they had always been harsh and arrogant, carried their brows very high against all the nations, and thought themselves hard to stand against.

But those who were so bold, swollen with thoughts beyond what is human, give way to womanish tears and compose a lament over themselves, broken down to weakness before they have even tasted battle. “For my loins are filled with faintness, and pangs have seized…” (Isaiah 21:3)
